To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

Canadian media experienced a twenty-first century discovery about China in 2004-2005, and that the volume of coverage of China's economy spiked and the volume of coverage about China's political rights declined.

the volume of media coverage of China increased significantly in the mid-2000s and that this increase was accompanied by a decline in coverage of human rights and democracy issues, while coverage of Japan decreased over the same time period and this decline was accompanied by a rise in coverage of human and civil rights issues.
the volume and tone of Canadian news coverage of China changed dramatically between 2000 and 2015, but these shifts in coverage did not necessarily lead to shifts in public opinion about China.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of whether Canadian media coverage of Japan and China has changed since the turn of the century and, if so, whether these changes are related to changes in Canadian attitudes.
the role of the media in shaping Canadian attitudes toward China and Japan, and how the media frames the news to the public.
the relationship between media frames of China and Japan, and the Canadian public's perceptions of these countries.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the Canadian media's coverage is not the cause of negative Canadian attitudes toward China, but rather that it has become a reflection of them.
Canadian media coverage is a weak predictor of Canadian public opinion.
Canadian media coverage is not an important determinant of public opinion.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Canadian media's portrayal of China has changed over the last 15 years, and this change has not had the intended effect of changing Canadian public opinion.

the Canadian media's coverage is not the primary cause of the decline in bilateral relations with China, and that the media's coverage of Japan is more closely tied to public opinion than that of China.
the Canadian media has been covering China in a way that is more positive than the Canadian public.
The main takeaway from our work is that
media coverage of China in the Canadian context has changed dramatically over the last 20 years and that these changes have not had the expected effect on public opinion.
the Canadian public's attitudes are not as malleable as policymakers and Chinese officials believe, and that Canadian foreign policy is not as reactive as some might assume.
